title: American attitudes toward nudges
abstract: Abstract To successfully select and implement nudges, policy makers need a psychological understanding of who opposes nudges, how they are perceived, and when alternative methods (e.g., forced choice) might work better. Using two representative samples, we examined four factors that influence U.S. attitudes toward nudges – types of nudges, individual dispositions, nudge perceptions, and nudge frames. Most nudges were supported, although opt-out defaults for organ donations were opposed in both samples. “System 1” nudges (e.g., defaults and sequential orderings) were viewed less favorably than “System 2” nudges (e.g., educational opportunities or reminders). System 1 nudges were perceived as more autonomy threatening, whereas System 2 nudges were viewed as more effective for better decision making and more necessary for changing behavior. People with greater empathetic concern tended to support both types of nudges and viewed them as the “right” kind of goals to have. Individualists opposed both types of nudges, and conservatives tended to oppose both types. Reactant people and those with a strong desire for control opposed System 1 nudges. To see whether framing could influence attitudes, we varied the description of the nudge in terms of the target (Personal vs. Societal) and the reference point for the nudge (Costs vs. Benefits). Empathetic people were more supportive when framing highlighted societal costs or benefits, and reactant people were more opposed to nudges when frames highlighted the personal costs of rejection.

claims.text: Most evaluated nudges were supported by U.S. participants across both representative samples, with default organ donation being consistently opposed.
System 2 nudges received significantly greater support than System 1 nudges.
System 1 nudges were perceived as more threatening to autonomy and more paternalistic than System 2 nudges.
System 2 nudges were perceived as more effective for good decision making, more necessary for changing behavior, sending the right message, and having the right goals compared to System 1 nudges.
The effect of nudge type on support was mediated by perceptions of threat to autonomy, effectiveness for good decision making, and necessity for changing behavior.
Individualism negatively correlated with support for both System 1 and System 2 nudges across both studies.
Desire for control and reactance were negatively correlated with support for System 1 nudges.
Overall support for nudges was not significantly affected by framing manipulations targeting personal versus societal impact or costs versus benefits.
People with greater empathy were significantly more supportive of nudges when framed around societal effects rather than personal effects.
Within personal frames, reactant individuals showed greater opposition to nudges framed in terms of costs of rejection compared to benefits.
Judged likability of companies implementing nudges was significantly higher for companies implementing System 2 nudges than System 1 nudges.

limitations.text: Results depend directly on the specific nudges selected for examination, and there are no guarantees that findings will generalize to other nudges.
Comparability between System 1 and System 2 nudges in matched pairs was not exact.
In the regression across all four frames, the interaction between reactance and the Personal/Cost frame did not reach statistical significance (t(197) = 1.82, p = 0.16).
Prior work by Tannenbaum et al. (2014) selected nudges on partisan appeals, finding partisan nudge bias where attitudes depended on the policymaker or political objective.

future_work.text: Investigate whether increasing public understanding of the actual effectiveness of System 1 nudges would increase or decrease their perceived threat to autonomy.
Examine the risks and efficacy of personalizing nudges to individual beliefs and preferences without triggering reactance.

methodologies.name: Representative Survey Study 1
methodologies.description: Evaluated public support and perceptions of 13 nudges (9 System 1, 4 System 2) alongside individual disposition scales in a representative sample of 250 U.S. adults.

methodologies.name: Representative Survey Study 2 with Factorial Framing
methodologies.description: Evaluated 10 matched nudges across five domains within-subjects, crossed with a 2 (Personal vs. Societal) x 2 (Cost vs. Benefit) between-subjects framing manipulation in 800 U.S. adults.
conditions: 5 policy domains (Medical Coverage, Retirement Savings, Credit Cards, Organ Donation, Water Conservation)
